oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Learning from Black Girls' Literacies of Love
oai_dc:dc.dc:creator: Barrett Rosser
oai_dc:dc.dc:subject: reflection
black girl literacies
love
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Black girls face violence in school spaces, making self-love a radical act within a white supremacist capitalist society. Grounded in Black feminist epistemologies and practitioner research, this study asks: What happens when high school-aged Black girls are engaged in an out-of-school inquiry group to read, write, and talk about the practice of love? Drawing on qualitative data, including field notes, transcripts from interviews and inquiry group sessions, and multimodal artifacts created by 13 girls from my larger dissertation study, I use qualitative analysis, including coding and collaborative descriptive reviews, while privileging the epistemologies of the girls to make sense of their knowledge and practice of love. Findings highlight how the girls enacted reflection, a Black Girls’ Literacies of Love (BGLoL), as a conduit to loving themselves and others. The implications emphasize the importance of reflection in schools as a tool to shape teacher practice and to create humanizing literacy experiences, especially for and with Black girls.
